rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active Form I reading means you return and assigns people agency, unlike the standard passive you are returned.
rows.anchor: restores human agency to the act of returning, contrasting with standard passive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading is the Form I perfect active verb khalaqa.
rows.anchor: Standard reading: Form I perfect active.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical innīya with fatḥa and innī with sukūn differ phonologically in pause or connection, with no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Fatḥa on yāʾ (inniya) vs. sukūn (innī) — canonical variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form IV nunsikh means God causes abrogation or copying, introducing an intermediary, unlike Form I nansakh, we abrogate.
rows.anchor: Form IV introduces an intermediary: God causes someone else to perform the abrogation

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads from n-s-ʾ, we defer it, rather than n-s-y, we cause it to be forgotten; the variant implies postponement rather than cognitive erasure.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathīr: root n-s-ʾ (to defer/delay) replaces n-s-y (to forget)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads the Qurʾān without hamza, softening the glottal stop in a canonical pronunciation.
rows.anchor: Without hamza — softening of the glottal stop, a well-attested canonical reading (Ibn Kathīr)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten-reader variant has ḍamma on the sīn in al-yusura instead of sukūn; it is a fuller phonetic form without semantic change.
rows.anchor: With ḍamma on sīn instead of sukūn — fuller phonetic form, no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A parallel ḍamma on the sīn in al-ʿusura creates a symmetrical fuller phonetic variant alongside al-yusura.
rows.anchor: With ḍamma on sīn — fuller phonetic form paralleling al-yusura; symmetric variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form II tukammilū rather than Form IV tukmilū emphasizes thorough, meticulous completion.
rows.anchor: Form II (tukammilū) instead of Form IV (tukmilū) — intensive completion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical vowel variant changes the hāʾ of fīhimā from kasra to ḍamma, with both dual pronoun forms grammatically valid.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: kasra to ḍamma on hā — fīhimā (standard) vs fīhumā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A dot variant changes bāʾ to thāʾ, changing k-b-r greatness to k-th-r abundance: the sin is abundant rather than great.
rows.anchor: Dot-variant: bā' → thā' shifts k-b-r (greatness) to k-th-r (abundance)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative al-ʿafwu reading treats it as subject or predicate, while accusative al-ʿafwa is an object reading, restructuring the syntax.
rows.anchor: Nominative variant: al-ʿafwu (ḍamma) = subject/predicate reading vs al-ʿafwa (fatḥa)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long ā variant in Ibrāhām replaces ī in the penultimate syllable, reflecting dialectal variation in Arabizing the Hebrew name; both readings are canonical.
rows.anchor: Long-vowel variant — ā instead of ī in penultimate syllable. Reflects dialectal variation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This instance likewise has the long ā variant instead of ī, consistently reflecting the same dialectal reading.
rows.anchor: Long-vowel variant ā replacing ī — identical to word 6 variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A quiescent yāʾ gives rabbī, while open yāʾ gives rabbiya; the fatḥa form makes the declaration more emphatic.
rows.anchor: Quiescent yāʾ vs. open yāʾ — rabbī (possessive with sukūn) vs. rabbiya

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A lengthened final alif in anā is a dialectal pronunciation variant of the pronoun, without a stated semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Extended vowel (madd) on final alif — lengthened pronunciation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third Ibrāhīm instance receives the same long-vowel variant as the earlier two occurrences.
rows.anchor: Long-vowel variant — consistent with words 6 and 15. All three Ibrahim instances receive the same variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hamza variant changes how the glottal stop is treated in the name Isrāʾīl.
rows.anchor: Hamza variant — different treatment of the glottal stop in the name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inna reading is an independent assertion, Indeed I, rather than subordination, shifting the syntax into direct speech.
rows.anchor: Inna reading = independent assertion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant vocalization of the pronoun suffix is dialectal and does not alter meaning.
rows.anchor: Variant vocalization of the pronoun suffix — no semantic change, dialectal variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment records the base canonical anni reading with the standard pronoun suffix.
rows.anchor: Base canonical reading with standard pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilating hamza changes hayʾa to hayya, a phonological variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of hamza: hayʾa → hayya — phonological variant, no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle al-ṭāʾir means the flying one, shifting from a collective species noun to a singular agent.
rows.anchor: shifts from collective noun (species) to singular agent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The base ṭayran reading is an indefinite singular or collective form.
rows.anchor: Base canonical reading — indefinite singular/collective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle ṭāʾiran emphasizes flying as an act rather than the category of bird.
rows.anchor: emphasizes the act of flying over the species-category

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The base canonical reading has ḍamma on the bāʾ of buyūtikum.
rows.anchor: Base canonical reading with ḍamma on bāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The biyūtikum variant has kasra on the bāʾ and is a dialectal vowel variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Kasra on bāʾ — dialectal vowel variant, no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active Form II reading makes the earth itself perform the leveling, rather than being passively leveled.
rows.anchor: Active voice Form II with tāʾ-marbūṭa of ta-faʿʿul origin or imperfect active — the earth itself performs the leveling

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilating tāʾ into sīn yields Form V and a reflexive sense: the earth makes itself level upon them.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of tāʾ into sīn — Form V tataṣawwā with ta- assimilated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra on the mīm instead of ḍamma is a liaison vowel; some readers use it before a pause or consonant.
rows.anchor: Kasra on mīm instead of ḍamma — different liaison vowel; some readers use kasra

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun variant bihumu has ḍamma on hāʾ rather than bihimu, reflecting Hijazi and Tamimi dialectal voweling.
rows.anchor: Ḍamma on hāʾ (bihumu vs bihimu) — dialectal variation in pronoun voweling; Ḥijāzī vs Tamīmī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza elision in jāʾa with compensatory lengthening yields jā; this is canonical in the Seven readings.
rows.anchor: Hamza elision with compensatory lengthening — jāʾa becomes jā by dropping the hamza

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This variant softens or elides the initial hamza of aḥad while retaining the hamza of jāʾa.
rows.anchor: Hamza modification on aḥad — the initial hamza of aḥad is softened or elided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eliding hamza at the junction merges the two hamzas into a lengthened ā through canonical phonetic assimilation.
rows.anchor: Hamza elision with compensatory madd (lengthening) — the two hamzas at the junction merge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imāla tilts the fatḥa on jīm toward kasra, producing a sound between ja and ji for certain canonical readers.
rows.anchor: Imāla (vowel tilting) — the fatḥa on jīm tilts toward kasra

rows.speaker: Ḥamza and Kisāʾī
rows.claim: Ḥamza and Kisāʾī read Form I lamasa instead of Form III lāmasa, removing the reciprocal morpheme and indicating one-sided touching.
rows.anchor: reading of Ḥamza and Kisāʾī. Legally significant: Form I = one-sided touching

rows.speaker: Shāfiʿī
rows.claim: The Shāfiʿī view takes Form I as one-sided touching, so any skin contact breaks wuḍūʾ.
rows.anchor: Shāfiʿī: any skin contact breaks wuḍūʾ

rows.speaker: Ḥanafī
rows.claim: The Ḥanafī view takes Form III mutual engagement as a euphemism for intercourse.
rows.anchor: Form III = mutual engagement (Ḥanafī: euphemism for intercourse)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A liaison variant gives the next verse's initial hamza ḍamma instead of the usual linking kasra, without changing fatīlan's meaning.
rows.anchor: affects liaison between this ayah's final word and the next ayah's opening imperative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun suffix alternates from -him to -hum after kasra as a dialectal phonological variant, without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Pronoun vowel shift: -him to -hum; standard dialectal alternation in pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form II yunassiyannaka suggests repeated or intensive causing-to-forget, unlike Form IV's one-time causation.
rows.anchor: Form II intensive (tafʿīl) instead of Form IV — yunassiyannaka implies repeated/intensive causing-to-forget

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light form mayt contrasts with standard mayyit in intensity; mayt can describe something recently dead or not deeply or permanently dead.
rows.anchor: Light form mayt vs. standard mayyit — difference in intensification; mayt may refer to what has recently died

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light mayt form is repeated here, matching the earlier variant and keeping both occurrences consistently light.
rows.anchor: Light form mayt paralleling the variant at word 10 — consistent lightening across both occurrences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle jāʿilu replaces perfect jaʿala, paralleling fāliqu so both predicates in Beat A are participles.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: active participle jāʿilu instead of perfect verb jaʿala — parallels fāliqu in Beat A

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With jāʿilu, layl changes from the accusative object of jaʿala to a genitive iḍāfa construction, restructuring the syntax.
rows.anchor: In the jāʿilu variant, layl shifts from accusative (object of jaʿala) to genitive (iḍāfa with jāʿilu)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The junction reads hamza al-waṣl with ḍamma rather than kasra, a canonical phonetic variation in liaison between the words.
rows.anchor: Hamza al-waṣl read with ḍamma instead of kasra at the junction — a canonical phonetic variation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thumur variant has ḍamma on both syllables and makes the sense explicitly plural fruits rather than collective fruit.
rows.anchor: Ḍamma-ḍamma instead of fatḥa-fatḥa — thumur is the plural of thamar

rows.speaker: classical grammarians
rows.claim: Classical grammarians debate whether geminated mayyit means currently dying while simplified mayt means already dead; both are canonical.
rows.anchor: classical grammarians debate whether مَيِّت = currently dying while مَيْت = already dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person plural reading says We gather them rather than He gathers them, changing narration about God into direct divine speech.
rows.anchor: shifts from narrative about God to God speaking directly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active reading means you yourselves come out rather than you are brought out, shifting agency from divine extraction to autonomous emergence.
rows.anchor: Shifts agency from divine extraction to autonomous emergence. Canonical in 7 reading traditions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative maʿdhiratun can be a predicate, it is an exculpation, or a subject, an exculpation is our motive, rather than accusative.
rows.anchor: Nominative reading (marfūʿ with tanwīn) — shifts from accusative ḥāl/mafʿūl to nominative predicate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eliding hamza changes baʾīs to bīs, simplifying articulation without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza elision: baʾīs → bīs; simplifies articulation without semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A compressed short-vowel form may evoke biʾs as an abstract noun of wretchedness rather than an adjective.
rows.anchor: Short vowel + sukūn: compressed form; may evoke biʾs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bayʾas variant metathesizes hamza in an archaic morphological pattern while preserving the root consonants.
rows.anchor: Metathesis of hamza: faʿlas pattern; archaic morphological variant preserving root consonants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person plural they reason shifts the ending from a direct second-person challenge to commentary about the narrated group.
rows.anchor: shifts from direct audience challenge to third-person comment about the narrated group

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form IV yumsikūna indicates simple retention, while Form II yumassikūna conveys intensive, repeated grasping or effortful clinging.
rows.anchor: Form IV yumsikūna vs standard Form II yumassikūna — IV = simple retention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭayf evokes a phantom or apparition, whereas ṭāʾif retains the sense of an active circling agent.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: ṭayf (phantom/apparition) vs ṭāʾif (circling agent)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza in quriʾa is softened to yāʾ, a dialectal phonological variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza replacement: the hamza in quriʾa is softened to yāʾ — a phonological variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dropping the hamza between rāʾ and alif yields Qurān without the glottal stop, a canonical continuous-pronunciation variant.
rows.anchor: Hamza omission: the hamza between rāʾ and alif is dropped, yielding Qurān without glottal stop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra variant ʿidwa alongside standard ʿudwa is a dialectal vowel alternation; both mean valley-bank.
rows.anchor: Kasra on ʿayn (ʿidwa instead of ʿudwa) — dialectal variant of the same word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same kasra variant at the second occurrence applies to both occurrences of ʿudwa.
rows.anchor: Same kasra variant as word 4 — applies identically to both occurrences of ʿudwa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unassimilated ḥayiya keeps the two yāʾs separate instead of geminating them; both forms are canonical seven-reader readings.
rows.anchor: Unassimilated form — ḥayiya instead of ḥayya; the two yāʾs are kept separate rather than geminated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Removing hamza from ʾatā produces yātī, smoothing pronunciation without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Hamza removal — ʾatā loses hamza, becoming yātī; smooths phonetic texture but no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waqf variant puts sukūn on the tāʾ when stopping and has no semantic impact.
rows.anchor: Waqf variant — pausal form with sukūn on tāʾ, standard in stopping

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The full yaʾtī form restores final yāʾ and removes apocopation, normalizing the verb to the indicative imperfect.
rows.anchor: Full form with final yāʾ restored — removes the apocopation, normalizing to standard indicative imperfect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The combined reading has yaʾt in pause and yaʾtī in continuation; both forms are canonical.
rows.anchor: Combined waqf/waṣl reading — yaʾt in pause, yaʾtī in continuation; both canonical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilating the tāʾ in lā takallamu creates idghām; the variant adds phonetic heaviness and gravity without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of tāʾ — lā takallamu becomes lā ttakallamu with idghām

rows.speaker: Ḥamza
rows.claim: Ḥamza reads biqya with short i on bāʾ and no yāʾ gemination; it may shift from lasting quality toward an act of remaining.
rows.anchor: Ḥamza reading: short i-vowel on bāʾ, dropping the tashdīd on yāʾ — biqya as a lighter nominal form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant retains the full final yāʾ in pause and connection, making the active participle morphologically complete without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ retained in pause and connection — canonical variant; makes the active participle morphologically complete

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waqf reading pronounces each of the letters separately, with sukūn or pause markers, emphasizing each as a distinct unit.
rows.anchor: Waqf reading: each letter separated with sukūn/pause markers — emphasizes individual pronunciation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn-for-ṣād pronunciation is linked to a possible Syriac etymology from strata, without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Sīn replaces ṣād — pronunciation variant reflecting the possible etymology from strata via Syriac

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām gives ṣād a slight zāy quality, producing a phonetic midpoint between ṣād and sīn; it is a canonical variant.
rows.anchor: Ishmām: the ṣād is pronounced with a slight zāy quality

rows.speaker: some readers
rows.claim: Some readers connect al-ḥamīdi to Allāhi in the genitive as an apposition or attribute, identifying the Praiseworthy as God across the verse boundary.
rows.anchor: Continuation into 14:2: some readers connect al-ḥamīdi directly to Allāhi (genitive)

rows.speaker: some readers
rows.claim: Other readers take Allāhu in the nominative as the subject of a new sentence beginning the next verse, syntactically separating it from al-ḥamīdi.
rows.anchor: Continuation into 14:2: Allāhu in nominative — beginning a new sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten-reader tradition attests both genitive and nominative linkage after al-ḥamīdi, making the verse boundary a site of variant parsing.
rows.anchor: 10-reader tradition attests both genitive and nominative linkage for Allāh after al-ḥamīdi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhām has fatḥa on hāʾ and long ā before mīm, reflecting Aramaic or Syriac phonology closer to Abraham; it is canonical among the Seven.
rows.anchor: Variant vocalization with fatḥa on hāʾ and long ā before mīm — reflects Aramaic/Syriac phonology

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant has explicit fatḥa on the yāʾ, lengthening the pronoun suffix phonetically without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Variant with explicit fatḥa on yāʾ — phonetic lengthening of the pronoun suffix; no semantic change
